core: Working definition of accounts payable: money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services it has already received on credit
How accounts payable arises: buying on credit from suppliers, documented by an invoice
The liability view: payables are obligations to pay, current liabilities on the balance sheet (liabilities detail belongs to the sibling topic)
Payment terms: net 30 and relatives (net 60, net 90), early-payment discounts such as 2/10, n/30
Managing payables: paying on time to preserve supplier trust and credit availability
Payable vs receivable: what the business owes vs what the business is owed (receivable detail belongs to the sibling topic)
Honest framing: payables are the business's promises, tracked as carefully as sales
supporting: Accounts payable agreements typically do not include interest, unlike notes payable
Accounts payable may be an open credit line between the supplier and the company
The invoice details the purchase, credit terms, invoice date, and shipping arrangements
Lenders and investors read current liabilities, including payables, to judge short-term cash needs
outOfScope: Statement of cash flows mechanics (sibling topic accounting:foundations:statement-of-cash-flows)
Journal entries, purchase discounts accounting mechanics, ratio analysis

claims.claim: Accounts payable is the money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services it has already received, purchased on credit.

Accounts payable arises when a business buys on credit: the supplier delivers goods or services now and agrees to be paid later, and the arrangement is documented by an invoice listing the purchase, credit terms, invoice date, and shipping arrangements.

Accounts payable is a current liability: it results from a past business activity, with payment due within a year (or the operating period), and is reported on the classified balance sheet among current liabilities.
Accounts payable agreements usually do not include interest, unlike notes payable; the arrangement may be an open credit line between the supplier and the company.

Payment terms such as net 30 set the full-payment deadline in days from the invoice date; variants like 2/10, n/30 offer a 2% discount for payment within 10 days, otherwise the net amount is due in 30 days.

Timely payment matters beyond avoiding fees: receiving payment on time lets the supplier free up cash and lowers the risk of nonpayment, which is why suppliers reward prompt payment with discounts and keep offering credit terms.
Accounts payable is the most common current liability, arising from a purchase not yet fully paid off or from recurring credit terms with suppliers.
A liability is an amount owed; forms of debt call for the borrower to pay back what is owed — accounts payable is the supplier-credit form of an amount owed.

Investors and creditors rely on proper reporting of current liabilities such as accounts payable to judge a company's cash needs; misreporting can lead decision-makers astray about short-term obligations.
Payables are the business's promises: they are tracked as carefully as sales because suppliers, lenders, and investors read them, and the businesses that keep their promises keep credit flowing.

positions: OpenStax: in many cases, accounts payable agreements do not include interest, unlike notes payable
Late or overdue payables can attract late fees or trigger stricter terms in practice
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Teach payables as typically interest-free supplier credit documented by invoice, while noting that missing the payment deadline can bring fees or tightened terms.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What is the most common payment term?
positions: OpenStax examples use 2/10, n/30 and 2/10, n/60 credit terms
Net 30 is the widely recognized baseline term, with net 60 and net 90 used for larger orders
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Present net 30 as the general named baseline ('net 30 and friends') and the discount variant as a common refinement; both sources agree terms are stated in days from the invoice date.
